headline: San Diego Says Goodbye to Camera Surveillance Program

levels.label: Grade 3-4
levels.summary: San Diego is a city in California. A few years ago, the city put special cameras on streetlights. These cameras could read license plates on cars. They were made by two companies called Flock and Ubicquia. The police said the cameras helped catch people who stole cars. Almost 700 stolen cars were found because of them. But many people worried the cameras watched everyone all the time, even people who did nothing wrong. A group called the Privacy Advisory Board warned the city that this could be a problem. Now, three years later, the city leaders changed their minds. They voted to stop using the cameras and take them down. This is not the first time San Diego tried this kind of camera system and then stopped it. A group that watches out for people's privacy across the country said many other cities have also canceled these camera deals. They believe people do not want to be tracked by the government while just going about their day.

levels.label: Grade 5-6
levels.summary: San Diego, California recently decided to remove special surveillance cameras from its streetlights. These cameras, made by a company called Flock, used artificial intelligence to automatically scan and read license plates on passing cars. A second company, Ubicquia, provided 'smart streetlights' that worked together with Flock's system. Police said the technology was useful: vehicle theft dropped 20 percent since 2023, and 689 stolen cars were recovered thanks to the cameras. Despite this success, the city council voted to end both programs completely. This decision is surprising because just three years earlier, the mayor and other city leaders had strongly pushed for these same cameras to be installed. Back then, a city group called the Privacy Advisory Board had warned officials not to approve the cameras, worried they could be used to track innocent people. One board member said she now feels 'vindicated,' meaning she feels proven right. She said cities should actually listen to expert advisory boards instead of ignoring their warnings. This is actually the second time San Diego has tried and then dropped smart streetlight cameras. An earlier version from a different company was shut down back in 2020. A privacy advocacy group based in Oakland, called Secure Justice, said they have tracked over 500 similar camera contracts being canceled across the United States, in cities led by both political parties. The group believes this shows that most Americans do not want to be constantly tracked by government cameras as they drive around their communities.

levels.label: Grade 7-8
levels.summary: The city of San Diego has decided to remove an entire surveillance system from its streets, including license plate reading cameras made by Flock and 'smart streetlight' technology made by Ubicquia. These two systems worked together: the streetlights had sensors and cameras, and Flock's artificial intelligence software automatically scanned license plates on passing vehicles, alerting police to cars connected to crimes. According to police representatives, the system contributed to a 20 percent decrease in vehicle theft and helped recover 689 stolen cars since 2023. Even with these results, the city council voted against continuing the program, reversing a decision made just three years earlier when the mayor and other officials had championed it. This is not San Diego's first experiment with streetlight surveillance technology. Years before Flock and Ubicquia, the city had installed thousands of similar smart streetlight systems from a company called GE Current, but a previous mayor shut that program down in 2020. When Ubicquia later purchased the platform and partnered with Flock to install 500 new cameras in 2023, the city's own Privacy Advisory Board objected, urging the council to reject it over concerns about mass surveillance and lack of oversight. The council approved it anyway at the time. Now, one board member, Pegah Parsi, says she feels vindicated by the recent reversal. She argued that cities should genuinely listen to expert advisory panels instead of dismissing their concerns, since ignoring warnings often ends up being more costly in the long run. This story reflects a larger, nationwide pattern. Secure Justice, a privacy advocacy organization based in Oakland, has tracked at least 513 similar Flock camera contracts being ended across cities in both politically conservative and liberal states. The group's director argues this trend shows that, regardless of political leaning, many Americans are uncomfortable with having their everyday movements automatically tracked and recorded by government-installed cameras. The debate highlights a tension that many communities face: balancing the benefits of technology that can help solve crimes against the risks of constant, automated surveillance of ordinary people's daily lives, raising questions about privacy, government power, and how much monitoring a community is willing to accept in exchange for safety.

levels.label: Grade 9-10
levels.summary: San Diego's city council has voted to completely dismantle a surveillance system that combined automatic license plate reader (ALPR) cameras from a company called Flock with 'smart streetlight' infrastructure from a company called Ubicquia. ALPR technology uses artificial intelligence to scan license plates on passing vehicles in real time, allowing police to quickly flag cars connected to crimes such as theft. According to police representatives, this system contributed to a 20 percent drop in vehicle theft since 2023 and helped recover 689 stolen vehicles. Despite these statistics, the council's vote represents a significant reversal: just three years earlier, the mayor and other city leaders had actively pushed for the program's approval and installation of 500 cameras in 2023. This is actually San Diego's second failed attempt at citywide smart streetlight surveillance. An earlier version, using thousands of devices from a different vendor called GE Current, was shut down by a previous mayoral administration back in 2020. When Ubicquia later acquired that smart city platform and partnered with Flock on a new rollout, the city's Privacy Advisory Board—an official watchdog group tasked with reviewing surveillance technology—formally recommended that the council reject the plan, citing privacy concerns. At the time, the council approved it anyway. One advisory board member, Pegah Parsi, has since written publicly that she feels 'vindicated' by the recent decision, arguing that cities should take their own expert advisory boards seriously rather than overruling them, since doing so can be far more costly down the road than simply heeding their advice from the start. This local story fits into a much larger national pattern. Secure Justice, a privacy-focused advocacy organization based in Oakland, has documented at least 513 Flock camera contracts being terminated across the country, in cities governed by both Democratic and Republican leadership. The organization's executive director, Brian Hofer, argues this widespread trend—spanning both politically red and blue areas—demonstrates that concerns about government surveillance cross partisan lines. He suggests that many Americans, regardless of political affiliation, are uncomfortable with the idea of their everyday movements being automatically logged and analyzed by government-installed camera networks as they drive through their own neighborhoods. This case illustrates an ongoing tension in modern policing and city governance: technology that demonstrably helps recover stolen property and potentially deters crime can simultaneously raise serious questions about mass data collection, who has access to that data, how long it's stored, and whether constant monitoring of public movement is an acceptable tradeoff for increased safety and law enforcement efficiency.

levels.label: Grade 11+
levels.summary: San Diego's city council has voted to dismantle an entire surveillance infrastructure combining Flock's automatic license plate reader (ALPR) cameras—which use artificial intelligence to scan and log license plates in real time—with 'smart streetlight' hardware supplied by a company called Ubicquia. Police representatives credited the system with contributing to a 20 percent decline in vehicle theft since 2023 and the recovery of 689 stolen vehicles, figures that would seem to justify continuing the program. Yet the council chose to end it anyway, marking a striking reversal from just three years prior, when the mayor and other city leaders actively lobbied for its approval and oversaw the installation of 500 cameras throughout the city in 2023. Notably, this is not San Diego's first attempt at large-scale streetlight surveillance, nor its first retreat from one. An earlier iteration, built on thousands of devices from a different vendor, GE Current, was shut down by a previous mayoral administration in 2020 after concerns arose about its use and oversight. When Ubicquia subsequently acquired that smart city platform and partnered with Flock to propose a renewed, more sophisticated installation, the city's own Privacy Advisory Board—an official municipal watchdog body responsible for reviewing surveillance technologies before adoption—formally urged the council to reject the plan, warning of the privacy risks inherent in constant, automated tracking of residents' movements. The council overrode that recommendation and approved the program regardless. Now, board member Pegah Parsi has publicly described feeling 'vindicated,' using the moment to argue more broadly that institutions which establish expert advisory boards should actually heed their guidance rather than treating such bodies as mere formalities, since ignoring expert warnings often proves far costlier than following them in the first place. San Diego's reversal is not an isolated incident but part of a broader national trend. Secure Justice, a privacy advocacy organization based in Oakland, reports having documented at least 513 Flock camera contracts terminated across the country, spanning cities in both politically conservative ('red') and liberal ('blue') states, as well as communities of vastly different sizes. The organization's executive director, Brian Hofer, contends that this geographic and political diversity is significant: it suggests that discomfort with government surveillance technology is not confined to any single ideological camp, but reflects a more widespread unease among Americans about being continuously monitored by automated government systems as they go about routine daily activities like driving to work or running errands. This case exposes a persistent and unresolved tension in contemporary urban governance—the conflict between leveraging data-driven technology to make policing more efficient and effective, and safeguarding civil liberties against the risks of pervasive, largely invisible mass surveillance, including questions about who controls the collected data, how securely it is stored, how long it is retained, and whether communities meaningfully consented to such monitoring in the first place or had it imposed upon them by officials eager to appear tough on crime.

questions: Do you think it's worth giving up some privacy if it helps police catch more car thieves? Why or why not?
If your school or neighborhood wanted to install cameras like these, what questions would you want answered before agreeing to it?
Why do you think it's important for leaders to actually listen to expert groups, like the Privacy Advisory Board, even when it's inconvenient or unpopular?
